The wing tip lift angle is now calculated per side. For the right wing the rotation.z value is positive, while the left wing uses a negative value so the tip rises correctly.

The wing rotation formula is finalized. Pitch is 0.1, sweep back is -0.42 times the side, and dihedral is 0.62 plus a flapping offset that is positive on the right wing and negative on the left.

Bank rotation is applied to the pose group rather than individual wings. When bank is positive, the crest side drops and the trough side rises. The pelican’s left wing faces the crest while its right wing faces the trough.

The right wing dihedral will be `0.62 + flap + bank * 0.35` and the left wing `0.62 + flap - bank * 0.15`, letting the body bank drive the lean while wings add a small differential. The body sphere will also be squashed to `0.82, 0.7, 1.2`.

A lighter breast sphere will sit in front of the body. The back and mantle will use a gray-blue tint to distinguish the white pelican body from its black primaries. A yellow eye patch will sit behind the eye, and a small yellow-orange bump on the upper bill will mark the signature breeding knob.

The author realized the American white pelican is an inland lake species, not a coastal surfer. The brown pelican is the correct choice for this ocean scene because it is the iconic diving bird of California and the sea. The brown pelican’s color palette is now being mapped out: pale yellow head, white front neck, chestnut brown back, gray-brown body, and dark brown-gray wings with silver-gray linings.

The brown pelican palette is now fixed. The head will be pale gold-white, the neck white, the nape chestnut brown, and the body warm gray-brown. Wing coverts are silvery gray, primaries near-black, and the upper bill yellow-olive. This dark-on-light contrast against the blue sea makes the bird instantly recognizable.

The bill tip is now a hooked red-orange, the pouch is brownish orange, and the feet are dark gray webbed. The eye will be pale yellow with a dark pupil. These colors create a distinct pelican silhouette against the sunset water.

The board will use bright cream, coral, and teal colors to separate the bird from the water. A chestnut sphere will mark the nape behind the neck tube. The bill tip is a downward-angled cone, and the lower mandible will show a small gap revealing the pouch edge. All files are ready to be written, installed, tested, served, and screenshot-checked.

The water grid will be 100 units wide with 180 segments, sized to 140 so the edges fade into fog at 70 units. Snapping the pelican to grid cells prevents vertices from sliding across the sine field and causing surface pops.

The water grid is 140 units wide with 180 segments, yielding about 32,000 vertices. The GPU can handle the twelve sine and power operations per vertex without issue.

Fog will fade from 40 to 90 units.

The sky will be rendered as a shader rather than a mesh. A sun disc will be drawn directly in the sky fragment shader to avoid clipping problems.

The sky shader now blends zenith, high, horizon, and below colors. It draws the sun disc with a sharp 900-degree power falloff and a softer glow. A horizon haze band adds warmth near the horizon. The sun direction vector will point from the camera toward the sun.

The sun direction vector will be normalized from the light position minus target. It will sit near y=0.28 to create a golden-hour disc above the horizon, placed off to the side for rim lighting. Directional light intensity is set to 2.4 with ACES exposure at 1.0 and hemisphere ambient at 0.55; these values will be tuned visually after the first screenshot. The brown pelican body avoids clipping that could occur with a white head.

The pelican head will use a pale gold tone rather than pure white. Roughness variation is being added to the materials. Small parts like the eye and bill will use low-segment soft spheres and cylinders. The bill will be shaped with a CatmullRomCurve3 tube instead of a simple cylinder.

The bill will be a tapered cylinder rather than a tube geometry, since tubes cannot easily be tapered. It will run from z = -0.75 to z = -1.65 for a long, prominent beak. A separate cone will form the hooked tip.

The bill will be parented to the head group so it moves with the head. It is built in local coordinates starting at (0, 0.02, -0.12) and ending at (0, -0.08, -0.95). The neck stays in pose space to avoid unwanted bend. The body and head groups are now clearly separated. Coding begins next.

A subtle camera roll will be added to the turns for dynamism. It is derived from bank and applied after lookAt, so it does not accumulate across frames. Camera position will also be smoothed with exponential interpolation.

Camera look-at target is smoothed with exponential interpolation. The pelican will snap to the wave surface each frame to avoid floating off the water, while the camera lags behind. A 200-particle system is being prepared using Float32Arrays for positions, velocities, and ages.

Spray particles will respawn at the tail or rail with random upward and outward velocities. Their age is set to 0.35–0.8 seconds, and gravity pulls them downward.

Spray particles will use soft white circles at size 0.18 with 70% opacity and normal blending, fading out of view when dead. Their respawn rate will scale with wave energy so the rail produces more foam during high surf.

Spray particles will use additive blending so their order does not matter. A simpler constant pool of 120 particles with short lives will replace the energy-based respawn logic.

A second directional fill light from the opposite side will provide cool shadow detail for the dark pelican body. The water will have a warm, translucent tropical-to-deep look with golden sunset reflections. A mist ribbon near the surfer was considered but skipped to avoid clutter.

The ride is named "sampleRide". The board's local nose points along the negative travel axis so it aligns with the wave. A comment will be added at the surface-alignment frame.

A `userData.nose` marker is placed at (0, 0.08, -1.2) on the board. A self-test asserts that the vector from this nose marker to the tail marker aligns with the travel direction.

A camera height check will keep the view above the water surface. The ride alignment uses flattened horizontal travel velocity projected onto the wave plane, ensuring the board faces the correct direction.

The board will sit slightly above the water surface by raising the rider along the surface normal. The board thickness is 0.09, with its center at y=0.06 in rider space and bottom near y=0.02. This keeps the board bottom skimming the surface while the center point contacts the wave. On steep faces the edges may intersect the water.

The board geometry will be offset by its bounding box so its bottom sits exactly on the water surface. The pelican feet will rest just above that top edge.

The pelican feet will be webbed extrusions rather than separate toe cones. Each foot is a dark gray shape extruded with depth 0.02 and rotated to lie flat on the board.

A `limb` helper will build short dark cylinders between the feet and body. The foot geometry is rotated to lie flat on the board with its forward axis pointing along negative z.

The limb helper aligns cylinder geometry to a direction vector using `setFromUnitVectors`. Legs will be parented to the rider rather than the pose group so they remain fixed on the board during banking. The body will pitch around a feet pivot while the feet stay anchored, with bank limited to roughly 0.3 radians and the body overlapping the hips.

The pelican hierarchy is now defined. A pivot group at y=0.38 anchors the body, and the pose group sits inside it. The body, wings, neck, head, and tail are built in local space and attached to the pose so their world transform stays intact when the pivot rotates.

The update loop will set the pivot group's pitch and bank rotations directly, since it is the single parent for both body and wings. Attaching body parts to the pose preserves their local rotation, so wing angles remain correct relative to the body.

The pivot rotation order is set to YXZ so pitch and bank combine cleanly. The tail will sit on the pivot so it lifts when the nose drops. Feet remain outside the pivot. No sound effects are planned. The animation will be silent.

The HTML page will declare English. The camera uses a 40-degree field of view with a near plane at 0.1 to compress the background and keep the pelican large. A resize listener updates the aspect ratio and renderer size. Logarithmic depth is being considered.

Logarithmic depth is unnecessary because the blob sits slightly above the water surface and avoids exact vertex overlap. The blob will use standard depth testing. Spray particles will render after the main scene with depth writes disabled. The canvas element will be styled at full width and height in CSS to match the renderer output.

CSS will set the canvas to full viewport size with a warm background and no overflow. Touch scrolling is disabled so the page stays non-interactive. Canvas textures will use SRGB color space. The board stripe is a mesh rather than a texture. A small orange nose patch will sit on the bill.

Clouds will be soft transparent spheres in sky-highlight colors, with no fog. The first screenshot composition will center the pelican behind a wave face, with spray trailing the board and the sun in the upper corner. The camera will sit low at height 2.6 and distance 9, angled slightly upward at the lip to fill roughly seventy percent of the frame with water and thirty percent with sky.

The camera will sit at y=1.7 and distance 7.2, looking at the pelican chest so the wave lip rises behind it as a sky band. This low-angle framing avoids clipping the wave between the camera and the surfer.

The camera will be pushed upward if it ever drops below the water surface by a small safety margin. The look target is offset slightly above the board so the pelican's head and beak stay fully in frame.

No extra foam meshes are needed; the shader foam is sufficient. The wave face uses a steep peaky derivative with an exponent of 1.55, creating a sharper crest and steeper lip. At phase π/2 + 0.52, the height evaluates to roughly 1.06, placing the surfer slightly below the crest. The phase range spans 0.52 radians around the neutral point.

The wave face is too shallow. The low point still sits near 0.62, so the surfer never drops far enough to show a clear up-and-down motion. I will deepen the wave profile so the surfer can reach the trough and mid-face.

The wave face is being reshaped with a skewed tanh curve instead of pure sine. This steepens the lip and deepens the lower face, giving the surfer a clear climb from roughly 0.32 to 1.28 in height.

Spray energy will spike at the wave lip and scale with speed. The particle system receives `lipAmount` and `speedEnergy` to drive burst intensity. Bank angle derives from the wave face's derivative.

Bank and pitch will be derived from the wave phase derivative. Bank is clamped to ±0.45 and pitch to ±0.2, with signs chosen so the pelican leans into the crest during climbs. The next step is to verify these values by screenshotting at a time when the phase derivative is strongly positive.

The wave profile will be sampled at several times to verify the climb and lip motion. Wing lift will spike briefly at the wave lip for a moment of balance. The water shader will gain a subtle ambient term so troughs are not completely black.

The water shader will blend deep blue, mid-blue, and face-white colors based on wave height. It adds warm diffuse light from the sun and a bright specular highlight.

The water shader now adds a subtle fresnel term and blends in white foam based on the foam value. The horizon color is set to a warm orange matching the sky. A sparse glint effect from the sun reflection is also included.

The wave shader will compute normals by finite differencing height at nearby points, ensuring they face the correct way. The board stripe and wave wrap logic must match exactly between JavaScript and GLSL.

A custom `wrap` helper will be added to both JavaScript and GLSL so wave phase wraps consistently, since GLSL `mod` always returns positive values while JavaScript `%` preserves the sign of the dividend. Time will pass as raw `t` and wrap per wave inside each module rather than pre-wrapping it differently.

The wave phase formula is being verified. It wraps the spatial projection and time independently, then subtracts them to produce a phase locked to the target value modulo 2π.

A `wrap2pi` helper will wrap wave phase to 0–2π so the sine function stays consistent even when individual components differ by multiples of 2π. The lip detection will use this wrapped phase near π/2.

javascript
for (const t of [0, 1, 10, 100, 10000]) {
  const { x, z, phase } = rideXZ(t);
  const ph = wrap2pi(wavePhase(0, x, z, t));

The wave phase is being verified against the target value modulo 2π, accepting a small tolerance. The wave parameters are being finalized with specific amplitudes, frequencies, and directional vectors.

The wave parameters are finalized with a long swell along the x-axis and a subtle amplitude. Foam wash on steep slopes is skipped, and debug axes will not be included. Antialiasing and DPR settings still need review, and the pelican model may require several iterations to look correct.

The pelican model will use a constants object at the top for easy proportion tuning. A hat or sunglasses was considered and rejected to keep the design natural and stylized. The beak will serve as the only facial expression.

The pelican wing tip will use four small dark boxes fanned outward instead of a single blob, giving the impression of individual primary feathers. Each box is placed along the wing's x-axis with slight rotation to spread them naturally.

The wing tip will combine a dark curved shape with the fanned feather boxes. The neck will be more S-shaped to give the pelican a tucked, dynamic profile against the forward-facing camera.

The camera sits behind and to the side of the pelican, roughly 3/4 profile. The forward vector is about (0.95, 0, 0.31) and the right vector is derived from that cross product with up. This places the camera at an azimuth offset of -7.2 along the forward axis and +4.6 along the right axis.

The camera will sit behind and slightly downhill from the pelican, placing it on the trough side at a rear 3/4 angle.

The camera behind the pelican would show the tail and back of the head, hiding the beak. A better framing is to place the camera ahead of the surfer on the trough side, looking back toward the face so the beak remains visible.

The camera will sit ahead of the pelican on the trough side, looking back at the face. This places the wave face behind the surfer and keeps the beak in frame.

The camera offset is set to 5.5 units ahead of the pelican, 4.8 units down the trough side, and 1.85 units up. This places the crest behind the surfer and keeps the beak in frame at roughly a 3/4 angle.

The camera will sit ahead of the pelican on the trough side, looking back at the face. This keeps the wave crest behind the surfer and avoids hiding the beak. The camera position is verified to remain clear of the wave lip, since the face slopes downward toward the trough. The plan is finalized with this front-side framing.

A camera angle check ensures the view stays ahead of the pelican. A second bird was considered and rejected. Clouds will sit on the crest side of the sky. A subtle vignette overlay will be added via CSS for a film-like finish.

The vignette will be a subtle radial gradient overlay with no pointer events, kept inline in the HTML. No text overlays will be added to preserve the cinematic look. The document title alone carries the title. I am now ready to write the files.

The wave constants are being written into `ocean.js`. Four sine components define the swell with specific amplitudes, wavenumbers, frequencies, and directional vectors. A `unit` helper normalizes direction vectors. The module exports these parameters as a `WAVES` object.

The `ocean.js` module is being implemented with a `wrap` helper and a `wavePhase` function that wraps spatial projection and time independently before subtracting them. A `peaky` function sharpens the sine wave using an exponent, and the `heightAt` function begins summing the four wave components.

The `surfaceNormal` function is being fixed to avoid mutating a shared default vector. Callers will pass their own target vector instead.

The shader strings will be exported from `ocean.js` as functions that read directly from the `WAVES` constants. In `ride.js`, a `CARVE` constant of 0.50 rad/s drives a `ridePhase` function that applies a `tanh` curve to the sine of time for smooth wave progression.

The `ridePhase` function maps the carve value to a wave phase near π/2, with a small offset and a 0.98 scaling factor. The `rideXZ` function computes the surfer's horizontal position from time and the wave phase, using a 6.5-unit per-second forward speed plus a 1.7-unit lateral sine oscillation. It derives vertical depth from the phase and the first wave's frequency-to-wavenumber ratio. Several reusable THREE.Vector3 scratch variables are being declared for the pelican's orientation calculations.

`sampleRide` is being implemented in `ride.js`. It samples the surfer's position at time `t` and a small forward offset to compute travel direction. The height and surface normal are fetched at that point. A phase delta between consecutive samples indicates whether the surfer is moving down the wave face.

Bank and pitch are clamped from the phase delta to keep the pelican upright. The lip value is derived from how close the wave phase is to π/2. `sampleRide` writes position, normal, travel, and these derived angles into the output object. `alignToSurface` then builds the local coordinate frame by normalizing the surface normal and the horizontal travel vector.

`alignToSurface` completes the pelican's orientation by projecting the travel vector onto the tangent plane, deriving the local right axis from the cross product of forward and up, and building a rotation matrix to set the object's quaternion. A `cameraFrame` helper is also being drafted to derive the camera's horizontal right direction from the surfer's travel vector.

`cameraFrame` is finalized. It derives the camera's right vector by crossing the horizontal travel direction with up and normalizing.

A review of `sampleRide` confirms no shared vector mutation: `rideXZ` returns plain objects, and the phase delta correctly reflects absolute change rather than accumulated error.

The helper still reuses module-level scratch vectors for travel and normal.

The module-level scratch vectors are confirmed safe to reuse across functions. `sampleRide` and `alignToSurface` do not alias each other's working vectors, so interleaved calls remain correct.

The main animation loop will call `sampleRide`, `alignToSurface`, and `cameraFrame` sequentially. Because each helper receives its own vector arguments, the shared `_fwd` scratch variable is not overwritten mid-call. The ride state object is being initialized with a `position` vector.

The ride state object is now fully initialized with position, normal, travel, and derived angles. The next files to write are Pelican.js and main.js. The surfaceNormal formula will be fixed to match the shader exactly. Water uniforms will be generated from the same wave constants to prevent phase drift between JavaScript and GLSL.

The water shader uniforms are being defined in `ocean.js`. They include the four wave peak values, directional vectors, a normalized sun direction, a horizon color, and a sixteen-element trail array of Vector2. The array is built with `Array.from` to match the GLSL uniform declaration.

The trail array will be seeded with the starting position so the wake does not draw from the origin. The vertex shader will pass foam intensity through a varying attribute. A separate pelican uniform is unnecessary because the trail already covers the body. The pelican's eyes will be wrapped in a group so their blink animation can scale without distorting the body position.

The pelican's eyes are being modeled as a group positioned at the head's forward and side offset. A white sphere forms each eye, and a tiny catchlight sphere sits just behind it to create a reflective highlight. Pupils will be drawn slightly toward the nose. A thin dark box above the eyes will serve as a brow shadow to help express emotion.

The eye design is being simplified to a yellow sphere with a black pupil and a white catchlight, dropping the dark ring idea. The head will be a pale gold sphere with a slightly flattened scale. A chestnut cap will sit on the upper rear of the head.

The chestnut cap is being placed as a child of the head mesh, offset slightly forward and upward so it frames the crown without obscuring the face. The pelican's body color is set to 0x6b5348, the wing coverts to 0x7e7368, and the primary feathers to 0x24282c.

The pelican model will include a lighter belly sphere and a dark brown tail. The `createPelican` function returns the root, pivot, wings, head, pouch, eyes, nose marker, and tail marker. The nose marker sits at the beak tip, and the tail marker marks the board tail. The skill requires the asset front to align with the board nose.

The board nose and beak both face negative z before bank rotation. After banking, the beak tip shifts slightly while the nose stays fixed.

Markers will sit on the root object: a nose marker at (0, 0.1, -1.15) and a tail marker at (0, 0.1, 1.0). The board forward vector will be normalized from their difference and must dot with travel above 0.9.

A separate beak tip marker will be a child of the head at the bill end. It will project onto the xz plane and dot with travel above 0.7.

A self-test will run once in the console to verify alignment and throw if it fails.

The page will have no user interface. A unit test is being written to verify that `alignToSurface` produces an orthonormal basis when the surface normal is tilted: the local y-axis should align with the normal, the local negative z-axis should align with the projected travel vector, and the axes must remain mutually perpendicular.

The `alignToSurface` unit test is complete. It asserts that the local y-axis aligns with the surface normal, the forward vector lies on the tangent plane, and it points toward the projected travel direction.

A board mesh will be placed under the pelican root at identity orientation, with its nose facing negative z. The pelican model will be written in `pelican.js` with shared geometry objects to keep memory usage low.

Wing geometries will be cloned before rotation so the left and right shapes remain independent. Frustum culling is enabled by default, but the water and spray particle systems will disable it because their bounding spheres follow the pelican as it moves.

Spray and sky meshes will both disable frustum culling. The sky will be drawn first with `renderOrder = -1` and `depthWrite: false` so it does not occlude the pelican.

Clouds will sit in front of the sky as transparent, depth-write-disabled meshes that follow the camera at a fixed height. The sky mesh will be repositioned to the camera each frame. The tonemapping include in the water shader is confirmed to expand automatically through THREE.ShaderMaterial.

The `toneMapped: true` flag may inject extra uniforms, so the installed Three.js source will be checked. The colorspace include requires pars attached by WebGLProgram, and a shader failure would render the screen black with an error in the console.

Baking a filmic curve into the shaders was rejected because it would break MeshStandardMaterial. The installed Three.js WebGLProgram source will be checked or fixed on runtime if shader includes fail. Lights will be added for the pelican's MeshStandardMaterial. Without an environment map, the material will look like clay with direct lighting.

The pelican material will use roughness 0.72 and zero metalness. The beak gets 0.38 roughness for a slight sheen, the pouch 0.55, and the eye 0.2. A fake shadow blob will be cast beneath the pelican.

Lighting is being tuned to ACES with exposure 1.05. The sky color is 0xffd0a8 and the ground is 0x1a4a5c at intensity 0.85. A directional light of 1.8 and a fill light of 0.4 from the crest side will keep shadows from looking crushed.

A private `package.json` will be created for the local install. A short comment header will be added to `main.js`. The animation will not respect reduced-motion preferences because the task requires motion. The loop avoids feeling repetitive by mixing a 12.6-second carve with a 39-second long swell and faster water chop, while the camera drifts continuously along the x-axis.

The camera drifts along x = 6.5 * t indefinitely. Float32 precision will hold for large positions, but jitter may appear after hours. Re-basing all positions to a moving anchor each frame would prevent this, though it is too complex.

The shader already wraps spatial coordinates with modulo, so large world positions will not jitter. Re-basing the pelican to a moving anchor was considered but rejected as unnecessary.

The shared vector bug in `surfaceNormal` will be fixed by removing the default shared vector. The ocean shader is being written with a `distToSeg` helper for wave geometry.

The `distToSeg` helper is now fully implemented in GLSL. The wake foam shader will blend 15 segments of the pelican's path into a fading band, with width scaling from 0.28 to 1.15 as each segment ages. A ring buffer or shift logic is being considered to manage the trail array.

The wake trail will use 20 points updated every 0.09 seconds, giving roughly 1.8 seconds of foam. This avoids the overhead of shifting the array every frame at 60 fps.

The wake trail will use 32 points instead of 24. The array shifts only when the pelican moves more than 0.55 units, so the foam length adapts to speed and avoids gaps. A 32-point vec2 uniform array is supported by Three.js.

The wake trail will be seeded at the pelican's tail position so foam does not streak from the origin. A local copy of the tail vector will be transformed to world space to avoid mutating the original.

The foam trail will omit a disc at the rider origin so no foam appears directly beneath the board center. The sky sun direction is fixed in world space as an upper-frame constant, keeping the lighting steady during the endless drift. This creates a continuous golden-hour effect.

The sun direction is fixed in world space at roughly (0.15, 0.42, 0.55), placing it slightly above and to the right of the pelican so it lights the face toward the camera. This avoids orientation-dependent adjustments as the pelican turns during carves.

The sun direction places the light behind and to the side of the camera, front-lighting the wave face that slopes toward the trough. This positions the light where it naturally hits the pelican’s body and catches the lip edge for specularity.

Birds will be added as simple decorative elements and removed if they look bad. Five cloud puffs will sit above the horizon. The pelican head group is placed at (0, 1.22, -0.62) with a pale skull sphere, chestnut cap, eyes, upper and lower bills, pouch, hook, and knob. The upper bill is modeled as a cylinder along the negative Z-axis slightly downward.

The upper bill cylinder is rotated to point slightly downward and forward. Its tip lands near world z = -1.54, well past the board nose at z = -1.2.

The beak tip will hover slightly above the board nose at z = -1.5, keeping it close to the board rather than sticking past the nose.

The surfboard is set to 3.1 units long with the nose at -1.55. Its width is 0.58 so the pelican's feet fit without looking cramped.

The board width is set to 0.64 so it reads clearly as a surfboard under the bird from the camera angle. The pelican's feet will sit at z = -0.05 and z = 0.28 with x offsets of ±0.12. The board geometry is being written as a THREE.Shape with the nose positioned at +y = 1.58.

The board shape is drawn with bezier and quadratic curves to form a classic longboard outline. It is extruded with beveling and rotated to lie flat on the ground, then translated so its bottom edge rests on the surface.

The board shape was traced clockwise, which would flip the extruded normals. The path is being rewritten to run counter-clockwise from the nose down the left side, around the tail, and up the right side.

The board shape is now traced counter-clockwise. The material will use DoubleSide so the extruded face is visible from both sides.

The board geometry will be extracted into a standalone function so it can be tested for correct normals without needing the document object. A script will average the Y component of every normal to verify the extrusion faces outward; if the average is negative, the shape winding or rotation will be flipped.

The surfboard will be built as two stacked meshes: a coral-colored rail layer scaled slightly larger in the X and Z axes and sitting just below the main deck, plus a cream-colored top deck.

The rail mesh will be scaled 1.035 in X and Z and 0.82 in Y, raised 0.01 unit above the deck to avoid z-fighting.

The rail mesh is now scaled to 0.55 in Y and raised 0.02 units so it sits in the lower half and peeks out the sides. A thin stringer box will run down the center of the board. The tail fin will be a small vertical box rotated slightly backward, placed just above the waterline.

A dark traction pad will sit on the tail of the deck. The remaining modules—spray, birds, clouds, and a self-test helper—are being prepared. The self-test will expose `window.__sceneTest` so the bundler can verify scene state.

The self-test will write dot-product results into `data-facing`, `data-cam`, and `data-above` attributes on the body element. Chrome’s `--dump-dom` flag can then extract these values without a visible DOM node.

Shader error checking is enabled so the renderer logs any compilation failures. The pelican model will be kept concise while still detailed. A neck tube will connect the body pivot to the head pivot, with the body center at (0, 0.66, 0.08) and the head at (0, 1.18, -0.72).

The neck tube is a 0.1-radius CatmullRom curve from the body pivot to the head pivot, colored cream. A chest sphere sits at (0, 0.58, -0.22) in a lighter brown-gold to catch light. Wings are tucked back at 50 degrees of sweep to keep the silhouette from looking like a crucifix.

Wing flapping will use a gentle sine blend at 1.35 and 8.5 Hz plus a slower 0.7 Hz pulse, opening wider when the pelican is high on a wave lip. The head will bob vertically and tilt slightly with pitch and bank. The pouch will squash and stretch rhythmically.

Pouch scale will be stored in `userData` to avoid double-scaling each frame. Antialiasing and a minimum pixel ratio of 2 are enabled. The HTML entry point is confirmed as an ES module, and a meta color-scheme tag is added. A README will explain how to view the page offline. Only the esbuild self-test is run; no bundler output is generated.

The pelican material will use DoubleSide only on the wings, and shadow receive will be disabled. Eye positions are set in local head space at (±0.09, 0.03, -0.14) so both eyes remain visible from a three-quarter view.

The pupil sits at (0, 0, -0.03) inside each eye group so it rests on the front of the eye. A small white catchlight is placed at (0.015, 0.015, -0.032). The lower bill is modeled as a cylinder rotated downward and positioned slightly below the upper beak.

The pouch is a sphere at (0, -0.12, -0.42) with scale 0.72 × 0.85 × 1.25. The upper bill knob is a smaller sphere at (0, 0.02, -0.72). Bird decorations may be dropped to keep the focus on the pelican alone.

Two distant birds and a sun glare on the water will be added. The ride is slowed to surf speed 5.5 and carve 0.42 for a graceful feel. Camera lerp uses an exponential decay of 0.25 per frame with slight roll from bank. A minimum camera height will be enforced. An inline Node test script will verify the build, and the Chrome binary will be located for screenshots.

The piece is judged on visual quality, so the pelican must read clearly and the scene composed. I will iterate screenshots to refine proportions, colors, camera, wave size, and lighting. MeshPhysicalMaterial sheen with a warm cream tint may give the feathers a soft, feathery finish.

MeshPhysicalMaterial with sheen is being applied to the pelican plumage for a soft feathered look. The beak will use a standard physical material with clearcoat for keratin gloss. These properties are confirmed to be available in the installed Three.js version.

The pouch material will use only color and roughness, skipping transmission to avoid expensive thickness calculations. A comment will be added to ocean.js linking the GLSL height shader to the JavaScript heightAt function, ensuring both sides share identical uniform values and math. The GLSL peak formula is verified against JavaScript, and Vector4 component access in GLSL is confirmed.

The ocean shader loop is being unrolled to four explicit wave terms. Dynamic indexing of the `vec4` amplitude uniform inside a loop could fail on WebGL1, so the GLSL and JavaScript height calculations will use fixed component access instead.

A `waveH` helper function will compute each wave term in GLSL using explicit float arguments, eliminating any dynamic indexing of the amplitude vector.

The shader will sample heightAt at three points per wave to compute surface slope. Foam will be generated only at the breaking lip by combining crest and slope with a wake effect, then clamped to the final foam output.

content.text: The scene is a golden-hour ride: a pelican carving a wave, camera following, everything generated in code so it still runs offline. I'll set up the modules and check the framing in a real render.

content.thinking:

name: long-running-background-tasks
description: >-
  Required reading before you start, watch, or wait on anything that keeps running after you launch it — background jobs, watchers, scheduled loops, CI, pull requests, training runs, dev servers, long builds. Read it before you launch such work and before you report on its state. Saying where a running job stands counts as working on it. Use when: about to launch, supervise, inspect, diagnose, or report on work that keeps running after it is started.
---

# Working with long-running background tasks

Only submitting or queuing jobs is not sufficient to complete the task. The definition of done is the job has completed successfully and you have verified that it has produced all the expected outputs.
10→
This means you must see through the jobs completion by watching the job to ensure that its healthy, progressing, and working as intended.

## Tools available

There's two ways to watch jobs: monitor and loop. Decide which of the two you need, sometimes you need both.

### monitor — deterministic, actionable events

- Use a monitor when the event is a predicate a script can evaluate — an API response, an exit code, a port answering.
20→- Typical events: CI turning red, a PR comment or merge conflict, a PR becoming ready to merge, a dev server coming up or going down, a job reaching a terminal state.
- The monitor requires a script polls on a fixed cadence and stays silent until the predicate fires, so an idle job costs nothing. More on writing good monitoring scripts below.
- Examples of when to use:
  - Monitoring a PR — wake on CI breaking, merge conflicts, etc.
  - Checking if local tooling is up — wake on the service being unavailable, errors, etc.
  - All of these wakeup cases can be checked deterministically.

### loop — qualitative health that needs reading

- Use a loop when judging health requires reading the logs and system information to detect failing, faulty or stalled jobs. It uses a subagent which is more expensive but more thorough.
30→- Typical signals: the loss curve going unstable, a filtering pipeline producing garbage, throughput quietly degrading, faulty nodes throwing CUDA errors.
- A subagent reads the logs on a fixed cadence (say every 10 min) and reports what changed, so it costs a wakeup every cycle.
- Examples of when to use:
  - Checking on a training or data processing job — the subagent should scan for instability, degradation, faulty nodes, etc.
  - Monitoring system deployment health — the subagent should scan for 4xx/5xx, response times, resources, etc.
  - All of these wakeup cases are hard to describe deterministically and hard to fully enumerate, so it is better to use a subagent to validate.

## Good monitoring scripts

The monitor tool wakes you up every time you log to stdout. Wakeups are expensive, so only log if there is something actionable — but log it as early as possible, since staying silent delays the task. Plan accordingly: minimize the number of wakeups while still firing them as quickly as possible.
40→
### Planning

- Enumerate all terminal conditions.
  - For PRs, this includes the PR being merged or closed.
  - For long-running jobs, this includes the job completing or unrecoverable failures.
- Enumerate all other situations where a wakeup is needed.
  - For PRs, this would include when a comment arrives (there are four different types of PR comments), when CI fails, when a merge conflict arises, and when the PR becomes ready to merge (CI green, no conflicts, reviews complete, no blockers).
  - For an ML training job, this can be when the loss is unstable or the instance is preempted.
- Determine situations where the monitoring has to update what it is tracking. For example, for monitoring PRs, the latest commit hash may change as you push new commits.
50→
### Writing

- The monitoring script should poll every 30s. `watch_pr.py` defaults to
  `--poll-interval 30`. Lower intervals cause GitHub rate limits, especially
  with more than one watcher on the same token.
- Based on the planning, exit immediately on terminal conditions with FAILED, DONE, or CANCELLED, and log ACTION_REQUIRED for wakeups.
- Send all debug diagnostics — both your watcher's own trace and the monitored job's output — to a file, so a log line can never be mistaken for DONE, FAILED, or CANCELLED.
- The script should fail as early as possible. Emit a FAILED token immediately when any required condition reaches terminal failure. For example, if you are waiting on CI and any of them fail, emit FAILED immediately.
- Write the script to a durable location such as ~/.grok and name it something clear such as `ci_watcher.sh`.
60→- Key every log file the script writes on the pid or session id of the thing being watched. The paths are otherwise fixed, so a second job of the same kind silently clobbers the first one's log.

## Handling wake-ups

- Address errors or actionable events immediately. Look through the logs and debug the issue thoroughly before settling on a root cause, as long-running processes are generally expensive. Resubmit the job once it is fixed:
  - For PRs, this means repushing the changes and restarting CI (if needed).
  - For jobs, requeue or relaunch the job.
  - Always restart the monitor or loop so that it points at the new PR or job.
- If there are multiple jobs running, start debugging immediately when any jobs fail. Minimize total wall-time with completing tasks.

70→## Restarts

- Whenever you relaunch a job, always update the monitor.
- Monitors have a maximum 10-hour time limit, so be sure to restart them if you hit the time limit and if the task being monitored is still running.
- When you spawn a new monitor, make sure to kill any previous ones that the new one replaces. For example, if you fix a training run and respawn it, be sure to kill previous monitors, as irrelevant wakeups are expensive.

## Cleanup

- If a monitor is in a terminal state, kill the monitor, the loop, and the job. Dangling processes such as unkilled broken training runs are expensive. Then, address all issues if present.
- If an outdated monitor wakes you — that is, it is attached to an old or dead run — make sure to kill it.
80→- Do not leave detached workers, duplicate pollers, or orphaned watcher processes behind.

## Examples

### Example: maintaining a dev server

Suppose you just made some changes to the user's frontend code and would like to spin it up to test it. While you're testing it, you would like to know if the server goes down for any reason (if you made changes, for example). This is a great use case for the monitor tool. First start a React app in a background terminal, which reports its pid:

```
run_terminal_command(
90→  command="echo $$; npm start >~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/dev_server_$$.log 2>&1",
  timeout=0,
  description="Start the dev server on :3000",
  background=true
) # prints the pid 123456789
```

There are no terminal states, but there are two actionable events from the watcher: `http://localhost:3000` coming up and going down.

You want to be notified as soon as it is up so you can use it, and you want to be woken when it stops so you can address it — fix the code, restart the server, free the port. Both down paths quote the tail of the server's log, so the wakeup arrives with the error already in hand. Polling every 5s is a good cadence since you want to quickly fix it if it is down, and it is not expensive to poll.
100→
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Log paths are keyed on the server pid so two dev servers cannot clobber each other.
PID=$1 URL=http://localhost:3000 DIR=~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks
LOG=$DIR/dev_server_$PID.log
up() { curl -fsS -o /dev/null --max-time 5 "$URL" 2>>"$DIR/watch_dev_server_$PID.log"; }
why() { tail -20 "$LOG" | tr -d '\r' | tr '\n' ' '; }

until up; do
110→  kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null || { echo "FAILED: pid $PID exited before $URL came up: $(why)"; exit 1; }
  sleep 5
done
echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $URL is up"

while :; do
  sleep 5
  up || { echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $URL is down: $(why)"; until up; do sleep 5; done; }
done
```
120→
To spawn the monitor, point it at the pid `npm start` reported:

```
monitor(
  command='bash ~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/watch_dev_server.sh 123456789',
  description="Watch the dev server on :3000"
)
```

130→On the first wakeup the app is ready to use and you can start testing it. After that, you may be woken up if the server goes down. When you do:
- Read `~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/dev_server_<pid>.log` for the full compile error or port conflict and fix it.
- If the dev server survived, hot reload picks the fix up and the watcher recovers on its own, so leave the monitor running.
- If the process is dead, restart it with a fresh `run_terminal_command`, then kill this monitor and spawn a new one against the new pid.

### Example: PR monitoring

PR monitoring should stop when the PR is merged or closed, and it should wake up on:
- For comments, you should ask users how they would like to resolve them (which ones to address automatically, whether to respond / resolve, etc.), then store the decision for new future sessions. There are four different types of PR comments.
  - Inline review threads
140→  - Review bodies
  - Conversation comments
  - Commit comments
- Failing CI - most can be fixed in the code but sometimes they may be flaky. For flaky CI, just rerun them.
- Merge conflicts
- The PR becoming ready to merge — CI passes, no merge conflicts, reviews complete, no blockers, no unresolved inline threads. That wakeup is `kind: mergeable`. Tell the user they can merge now. It is not terminal; keep watching until merge or close.

You can find the example script bundled with this skill at watch_pr.py. It needs an authenticated `gh` CLI (`gh auth login`) and `python3`. Default poll is 30s; a lower poll rate may hit GitHub rate limits at higher concurrency. Transport errors (timeouts, resets, DNS) retry with backoff and jitter and do not print a line.

```
150→monitor(
  command='python3 ~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/watch_pr.py "https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build/pull/123"',
  description="Watch PR 123"
)
```

### Example: training monitoring

For monitoring long training jobs, the terminal conditions are when the job either fails or completes. Further, many issues cannot be caught deterministically, so use a subagent to run a script for most of the high-level update, then scan the logs for errors such as faulty nodes or CUDA warnings.

160→The script below is bundled with this skill as watch_training.py. Run it with `--help` for every flag and for the run-directory and log-line layout it expects, since it parses nanoGPT stdout out of a Slurm run dir.

```md
Keep an eye on the nanoGPT run nanogpt_owt_124m_r1 (slurm job 1234567) and tell me what changed since last time. Worktree ~/worktrees/nanogpt-owt-124m.

1. python3 ~/.grok/skills/long-running-background-tasks/watch_training.py --run-name nanogpt_owt_124m_r1 --job-id 1234567 --target-val 3.00

How to report:
- Start with the job's state and if it changed, e.g. "still RUNNING" or "PENDING -> RUNNING".
- Copy the ISSUES line and the STATUS line from the monitor exactly as it is written, numbers and all. STATUS will include where the run is heading: how far along, iters left, the eta, and whether val loss is still coming down. We want val loss at or under 3.00.
170→- If the state didn't change, tell me that in one line and stop.
- If the job has finished or died, give me the state, the exit code, and the last ISSUES, and run these two for me:
  sacct -j 1234567 -D -X -P -o JobID,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode,Elapsed,NodeList,FailedNode
  tail -20 ~/train_logs/slurm-nanogpt_owt_124m_r1-1234567.out

Keep <=10 lines: state, progress and eta, loss trend, then anything that smells like training going unstable (loss spiking, NaN, val loss creeping back up) or the cluster misbehaving (a drained or failing node, OOM, NCCL errors, a preemption, iters suddenly slower than usual).
```

Launch the scheduler on a 10 min interval, and spawn a monitor to be notified when the job crashes or succeeds.

180→```
scheduler_create(
  interval="10m",
  prompt: "...", # Copy from the prompt above.
)
monitor(
  # Wakes on pending/running/finished changes after the first observation.
  # First poll is silent unless the job is already COMPLETED or failed —
  # PENDING matches *ING, so treating an empty previous state as a
  # transition would wake immediately on a just-submitted job.
190→  command='J=1234567; p=; while :; do s=$(sacct -nXP -j $J -o State|head -1); s=${s%% *}; s=${s:-PENDING}; if [ "$s" != "$p" ]; then case $s in COMPLETED) echo "DONE: $J"; exit;; PENDING|RUNNING|CONFIGURING|COMPLETING|REQUEUED|SUSPENDED|RESIZING) [ -n "$p" ] && echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $J $p -> $s";; *) echo "FAILED: $J $s"; exit 1;; esac; fi; p=$s; sleep 30; done',
  description="Watch training run"
)
```

Launch both, so that we know when the job completes. When the monitor reports that the job has completed, cancel both the monitor and the scheduler, then determine next steps. Then:
- If it succeeded, simply present the results to the user.
- If it failed, debug the issue thoroughly, then fix and relaunch the job with new monitors attached. Make sure to have a thorough understanding of the issue before resubmitting, since training jobs are expensive. But always relaunch jobs so you don't waste the user's time.

# Working with long-running background tasks

Only submitting or queuing jobs is not sufficient to complete the task. The definition of done is the job has completed successfully and you have verified that it has produced all the expected outputs.

This means you must see through the jobs completion by watching the job to ensure that its healthy, progressing, and working as intended.

## Tools available

There's two ways to watch jobs: monitor and loop. Decide which of the two you need, sometimes you need both.

### monitor — deterministic, actionable events

- Use a monitor when the event is a predicate a script can evaluate — an API response, an exit code, a port answering.
- Typical events: CI turning red, a PR comment or merge conflict, a PR becoming ready to merge, a dev server coming up or going down, a job reaching a terminal state.
- The monitor requires a script polls on a fixed cadence and stays silent until the predicate fires, so an idle job costs nothing. More on writing good monitoring scripts below.
- Examples of when to use:
  - Monitoring a PR — wake on CI breaking, merge conflicts, etc.
  - Checking if local tooling is up — wake on the service being unavailable, errors, etc.
  - All of these wakeup cases can be checked deterministically.

### loop — qualitative health that needs reading

- Use a loop when judging health requires reading the logs and system information to detect failing, faulty or stalled jobs. It uses a subagent which is more expensive but more thorough.
- Typical signals: the loss curve going unstable, a filtering pipeline producing garbage, throughput quietly degrading, faulty nodes throwing CUDA errors.
- A subagent reads the logs on a fixed cadence (say every 10 min) and reports what changed, so it costs a wakeup every cycle.
- Examples of when to use:
  - Checking on a training or data processing job — the subagent should scan for instability, degradation, faulty nodes, etc.
  - Monitoring system deployment health — the subagent should scan for 4xx/5xx, response times, resources, etc.
  - All of these wakeup cases are hard to describe deterministically and hard to fully enumerate, so it is better to use a subagent to validate.

## Good monitoring scripts

The monitor tool wakes you up every time you log to stdout. Wakeups are expensive, so only log if there is something actionable — but log it as early as possible, since staying silent delays the task. Plan accordingly: minimize the number of wakeups while still firing them as quickly as possible.

### Planning

- Enumerate all terminal conditions.
  - For PRs, this includes the PR being merged or closed.
  - For long-running jobs, this includes the job completing or unrecoverable failures.
- Enumerate all other situations where a wakeup is needed.
  - For PRs, this would include when a comment arrives (there are four different types of PR comments), when CI fails, when a merge conflict arises, and when the PR becomes ready to merge (CI green, no conflicts, reviews complete, no blockers).
  - For an ML training job, this can be when the loss is unstable or the instance is preempted.
- Determine situations where the monitoring has to update what it is tracking. For example, for monitoring PRs, the latest commit hash may change as you push new commits.

### Writing

- The monitoring script should poll every 30s. `watch_pr.py` defaults to
  `--poll-interval 30`. Lower intervals cause GitHub rate limits, especially
  with more than one watcher on the same token.
- Based on the planning, exit immediately on terminal conditions with FAILED, DONE, or CANCELLED, and log ACTION_REQUIRED for wakeups.
- Send all debug diagnostics — both your watcher's own trace and the monitored job's output — to a file, so a log line can never be mistaken for DONE, FAILED, or CANCELLED.
- The script should fail as early as possible. Emit a FAILED token immediately when any required condition reaches terminal failure. For example, if you are waiting on CI and any of them fail, emit FAILED immediately.
- Write the script to a durable location such as ~/.grok and name it something clear such as `ci_watcher.sh`.
- Key every log file the script writes on the pid or session id of the thing being watched. The paths are otherwise fixed, so a second job of the same kind silently clobbers the first one's log.

## Handling wake-ups

- Address errors or actionable events immediately. Look through the logs and debug the issue thoroughly before settling on a root cause, as long-running processes are generally expensive. Resubmit the job once it is fixed:
  - For PRs, this means repushing the changes and restarting CI (if needed).
  - For jobs, requeue or relaunch the job.
  - Always restart the monitor or loop so that it points at the new PR or job.
- If there are multiple jobs running, start debugging immediately when any jobs fail. Minimize total wall-time with completing tasks.

## Restarts

- Whenever you relaunch a job, always update the monitor.
- Monitors have a maximum 10-hour time limit, so be sure to restart them if you hit the time limit and if the task being monitored is still running.
- When you spawn a new monitor, make sure to kill any previous ones that the new one replaces. For example, if you fix a training run and respawn it, be sure to kill previous monitors, as irrelevant wakeups are expensive.

## Cleanup

- If a monitor is in a terminal state, kill the monitor, the loop, and the job. Dangling processes such as unkilled broken training runs are expensive. Then, address all issues if present.
- If an outdated monitor wakes you — that is, it is attached to an old or dead run — make sure to kill it.
- Do not leave detached workers, duplicate pollers, or orphaned watcher processes behind.

### Example: maintaining a dev server

Suppose you just made some changes to the user's frontend code and would like to spin it up to test it. While you're testing it, you would like to know if the server goes down for any reason (if you made changes, for example). This is a great use case for the monitor tool. You want to be notified as soon as it is up so you can use it, and you want to be woken when it stops so you can address it — fix the code, restart the server, free the port. name: long-running-background-tasks
description: >-
  Required reading before you start, watch, or wait on anything that keeps running after you launch it — background jobs, watchers, scheduled loops, CI, pull requests, training runs, dev servers, long builds. Read it before you launch such work and before you report on its state. Saying where a running job stands counts as working on it. Use when: about to launch, supervise, inspect, diagnose, or report on work that keeps running after it is started.
---

# Working with long-running background tasks

Only submitting or queuing jobs is not sufficient to complete the task. The definition of done is the job has completed successfully and you have verified that it has produced all the expected outputs.
10→
This means you must see through the jobs completion by watching the job to ensure that its healthy, progressing, and working as intended.

## Tools available

There's two ways to watch jobs: monitor and loop. Decide which of the two you need, sometimes you need both.

### monitor — deterministic, actionable events

- Use a monitor when the event is a predicate a script can evaluate — an API response, an exit code, a port answering.
20→- Typical events: CI turning red, a PR comment or merge conflict, a PR becoming ready to merge, a dev server coming up or going down, a job reaching a terminal state.
- The monitor requires a script polls on a fixed cadence and stays silent until the predicate fires, so an idle job costs nothing. More on writing good monitoring scripts below.
- Examples of when to use:
  - Monitoring a PR — wake on CI breaking, merge conflicts, etc.
  - Checking if local tooling is up — wake on the service being unavailable, errors, etc.
  - All of these wakeup cases can be checked deterministically.

### loop — qualitative health that needs reading

- Use a loop when judging health requires reading the logs and system information to detect failing, faulty or stalled jobs. It uses a subagent which is more expensive but more thorough.
30→- Typical signals: the loss curve going unstable, a filtering pipeline producing garbage, throughput quietly degrading, faulty nodes throwing CUDA errors.
- A subagent reads the logs on a fixed cadence (say every 10 min) and reports what changed, so it costs a wakeup every cycle.
- Examples of when to use:
  - Checking on a training or data processing job — the subagent should scan for instability, degradation, faulty nodes, etc.
  - Monitoring system deployment health — the subagent should scan for 4xx/5xx, response times, resources, etc.
  - All of these wakeup cases are hard to describe deterministically and hard to fully enumerate, so it is better to use a subagent to validate.

## Good monitoring scripts

The monitor tool wakes you up every time you log to stdout. Wakeups are expensive, so only log if there is something actionable — but log it as early as possible, since staying silent delays the task. Plan accordingly: minimize the number of wakeups while still firing them as quickly as possible.
40→
### Planning

- Enumerate all terminal conditions.
  - For PRs, this includes the PR being merged or closed.
  - For long-running jobs, this includes the job completing or unrecoverable failures.
- Enumerate all other situations where a wakeup is needed.
  - For PRs, this would include when a comment arrives (there are four different types of PR comments), when CI fails, when a merge conflict arises, and when the PR becomes ready to merge (CI green, no conflicts, reviews complete, no blockers).
  - For an ML training job, this can be when the loss is unstable or the instance is preempted.
- Determine situations where the monitoring has to update what it is tracking. For example, for monitoring PRs, the latest commit hash may change as you push new commits.
50→
### Writing

- The monitoring script should poll every 30s. `watch_pr.py` defaults to
  `--poll-interval 30`. Lower intervals cause GitHub rate limits, especially
  with more than one watcher on the same token.
- Based on the planning, exit immediately on terminal conditions with FAILED, DONE, or CANCELLED, and log ACTION_REQUIRED for wakeups.
- Send all debug diagnostics — both your watcher's own trace and the monitored job's output — to a file, so a log line can never be mistaken for DONE, FAILED, or CANCELLED.
- The script should fail as early as possible. Emit a FAILED token immediately when any required condition reaches terminal failure. For example, if you are waiting on CI and any of them fail, emit FAILED immediately.
- Write the script to a durable location such as ~/.grok and name it something clear such as `ci_watcher.sh`.
60→- Key every log file the script writes on the pid or session id of the thing being watched. The paths are otherwise fixed, so a second job of the same kind silently clobbers the first one's log.

## Handling wake-ups

- Address errors or actionable events immediately. Look through the logs and debug the issue thoroughly before settling on a root cause, as long-running processes are generally expensive. Resubmit the job once it is fixed:
  - For PRs, this means repushing the changes and restarting CI (if needed).
  - For jobs, requeue or relaunch the job.
  - Always restart the monitor or loop so that it points at the new PR or job.
- If there are multiple jobs running, start debugging immediately when any jobs fail. Minimize total wall-time with completing tasks.

70→## Restarts

- Whenever you relaunch a job, always update the monitor.
- Monitors have a maximum 10-hour time limit, so be sure to restart them if you hit the time limit and if the task being monitored is still running.
- When you spawn a new monitor, make sure to kill any previous ones that the new one replaces. For example, if you fix a training run and respawn it, be sure to kill previous monitors, as irrelevant wakeups are expensive.

## Cleanup

- If a monitor is in a terminal state, kill the monitor, the loop, and the job. Dangling processes such as unkilled broken training runs are expensive. Then, address all issues if present.
- If an outdated monitor wakes you — that is, it is attached to an old or dead run — make sure to kill it.
80→- Do not leave detached workers, duplicate pollers, or orphaned watcher processes behind.

## Examples

### Example: maintaining a dev server

Suppose you just made some changes to the user's frontend code and would like to spin it up to test it. While you're testing it, you would like to know if the server goes down for any reason (if you made changes, for example). This is a great use case for the monitor tool. First start a React app in a background terminal, which reports its pid:

```
run_terminal_command(
90→  command="echo $$; npm start >~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/dev_server_$$.log 2>&1",
  timeout=0,
  description="Start the dev server on :3000",
  background=true
) # prints the pid 123456789
```

There are no terminal states, but there are two actionable events from the watcher: `http://localhost:3000` coming up and going down.

You want to be notified as soon as it is up so you can use it, and you want to be woken when it stops so you can address it — fix the code, restart the server, free the port. Both down paths quote the tail of the server's log, so the wakeup arrives with the error already in hand. Polling every 5s is a good cadence since you want to quickly fix it if it is down, and it is not expensive to poll.
100→
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Log paths are keyed on the server pid so two dev servers cannot clobber each other.
PID=$1 URL=http://localhost:3000 DIR=~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks
LOG=$DIR/dev_server_$PID.log
up() { curl -fsS -o /dev/null --max-time 5 "$URL" 2>>"$DIR/watch_dev_server_$PID.log"; }
why() { tail -20 "$LOG" | tr -d '\r' | tr '\n' ' '; }

until up; do
110→  kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null || { echo "FAILED: pid $PID exited before $URL came up: $(why)"; exit 1; }
  sleep 5
done
echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $URL is up"

while :; do
  sleep 5
  up || { echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $URL is down: $(why)"; until up; do sleep 5; done; }
done
```
120→
To spawn the monitor, point it at the pid `npm start` reported:

```
monitor(
  command='bash ~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/watch_dev_server.sh 123456789',
  description="Watch the dev server on :3000"
)
```

130→On the first wakeup the app is ready to use and you can start testing it. After that, you may be woken up if the server goes down. When you do:
- Read `~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/dev_server_<pid>.log` for the full compile error or port conflict and fix it.
- If the dev server survived, hot reload picks the fix up and the watcher recovers on its own, so leave the monitor running.
- If the process is dead, restart it with a fresh `run_terminal_command`, then kill this monitor and spawn a new one against the new pid.

### Example: PR monitoring

PR monitoring should stop when the PR is merged or closed, and it should wake up on:
- For comments, you should ask users how they would like to resolve them (which ones to address automatically, whether to respond / resolve, etc.), then store the decision for new future sessions. There are four different types of PR comments.
  - Inline review threads
140→  - Review bodies
  - Conversation comments
  - Commit comments
- Failing CI - most can be fixed in the code but sometimes they may be flaky. For flaky CI, just rerun them.
- Merge conflicts
- The PR becoming ready to merge — CI passes, no merge conflicts, reviews complete, no blockers, no unresolved inline threads. That wakeup is `kind: mergeable`. Tell the user they can merge now. It is not terminal; keep watching until merge or close.

You can find the example script bundled with this skill at watch_pr.py. It needs an authenticated `gh` CLI (`gh auth login`) and `python3`. Default poll is 30s; a lower poll rate may hit GitHub rate limits at higher concurrency. Transport errors (timeouts, resets, DNS) retry with backoff and jitter and do not print a line.

```
150→monitor(
  command='python3 ~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/watch_pr.py "https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build/pull/123"',
  description="Watch PR 123"
)
```

### Example: training monitoring

For monitoring long training jobs, the terminal conditions are when the job either fails or completes. Further, many issues cannot be caught deterministically, so use a subagent to run a script for most of the high-level update, then scan the logs for errors such as faulty nodes or CUDA warnings.

160→The script below is bundled with this skill as watch_training.py. Run it with `--help` for every flag and for the run-directory and log-line layout it expects, since it parses nanoGPT stdout out of a Slurm run dir.

```md
Keep an eye on the nanoGPT run nanogpt_owt_124m_r1 (slurm job 1234567) and tell me what changed since last time. Worktree ~/worktrees/nanogpt-owt-124m.

1. python3 ~/.grok/skills/long-running-background-tasks/watch_training.py --run-name nanogpt_owt_124m_r1 --job-id 1234567 --target-val 3.00

How to report:
- Start with the job's state and if it changed, e.g. "still RUNNING" or "PENDING -> RUNNING".
- Copy the ISSUES line and the STATUS line from the monitor exactly as it is written, numbers and all. STATUS will include where the run is heading: how far along, iters left, the eta, and whether val loss is still coming down. We want val loss at or under 3.00.
170→- If the state didn't change, tell me that in one line and stop.
- If the job has finished or died, give me the state, the exit code, and the last ISSUES, and run these two for me:
  sacct -j 1234567 -D -X -P -o JobID,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode,Elapsed,NodeList,FailedNode
  tail -20 ~/train_logs/slurm-nanogpt_owt_124m_r1-1234567.out

Keep <=10 lines: state, progress and eta, loss trend, then anything that smells like training going unstable (loss spiking, NaN, val loss creeping back up) or the cluster misbehaving (a drained or failing node, OOM, NCCL errors, a preemption, iters suddenly slower than usual).
```

Launch the scheduler on a 10 min interval, and spawn a monitor to be notified when the job crashes or succeeds.

180→```
scheduler_create(
  interval="10m",
  prompt: "...", # Copy from the prompt above.
)
monitor(
  # Wakes on pending/running/finished changes after the first observation.
  # First poll is silent unless the job is already COMPLETED or failed —
  # PENDING matches *ING, so treating an empty previous state as a
  # transition would wake immediately on a just-submitted job.
190→  command='J=1234567; p=; while :; do s=$(sacct -nXP -j $J -o State|head -1); s=${s%% *}; s=${s:-PENDING}; if [ "$s" != "$p" ]; then case $s in COMPLETED) echo "DONE: $J"; exit;; PENDING|RUNNING|CONFIGURING|COMPLETING|REQUEUED|SUSPENDED|RESIZING) [ -n "$p" ] && echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $J $p -> $s";; *) echo "FAILED: $J $s"; exit 1;; esac; fi; p=$s; sleep 30; done',
  description="Watch training run"
)
```

Launch both, so that we know when the job completes. When the monitor reports that the job has completed, cancel both the monitor and the scheduler, then determine next steps. Then:
- If it succeeded, simply present the results to the user.
- If it failed, debug the issue thoroughly, then fix and relaunch the job with new monitors attached. Make sure to have a thorough understanding of the issue before resubmitting, since training jobs are expensive. But always relaunch jobs so you don't waste the user's time.

# Working with long-running background tasks

Only submitting or queuing jobs is not sufficient to complete the task. The definition of done is the job has completed successfully and you have verified that it has produced all the expected outputs.

This means you must see through the jobs completion by watching the job to ensure that its healthy, progressing, and working as intended.

## Tools available

There's two ways to watch jobs: monitor and loop. Decide which of the two you need, sometimes you need both.

### monitor — deterministic, actionable events

- Use a monitor when the event is a predicate a script can evaluate — an API response, an exit code, a port answering.
- Typical events: CI turning red, a PR comment or merge conflict, a PR becoming ready to merge, a dev server coming up or going down, a job reaching a terminal state.
- The monitor requires a script polls on a fixed cadence and stays silent until the predicate fires, so an idle job costs nothing. More on writing good monitoring scripts below.
- Examples of when to use:
  - Monitoring a PR — wake on CI breaking, merge conflicts, etc.
  - Checking if local tooling is up — wake on the service being unavailable, errors, etc.
  - All of these wakeup cases can be checked deterministically.

### loop — qualitative health that needs reading

- Use a loop when judging health requires reading the logs and system information to detect failing, faulty or stalled jobs. It uses a subagent which is more expensive but more thorough.
- Typical signals: the loss curve going unstable, a filtering pipeline producing garbage, throughput quietly degrading, faulty nodes throwing CUDA errors.
- A subagent reads the logs on a fixed cadence (say every 10 min) and reports what changed, so it costs a wakeup every cycle.
- Examples of when to use:
  - Checking on a training or data processing job — the subagent should scan for instability, degradation, faulty nodes, etc.
  - Monitoring system deployment health — the subagent should scan for 4xx/5xx, response times, resources, etc.
  - All of these wakeup cases are hard to describe deterministically and hard to fully enumerate, so it is better to use a subagent to validate.

## Good monitoring scripts

The monitor tool wakes you up every time you log to stdout. Wakeups are expensive, so only log if there is something actionable — but log it as early as possible, since staying silent delays the task. Plan accordingly: minimize the number of wakeups while still firing them as quickly as possible.

### Planning

- Enumerate all terminal conditions.
  - For PRs, this includes the PR being merged or closed.
  - For long-running jobs, this includes the job completing or unrecoverable failures.
- Enumerate all other situations where a wakeup is needed.
  - For PRs, this would include when a comment arrives (there are four different types of PR comments), when CI fails, when a merge conflict arises, and when the PR becomes ready to merge (CI green, no conflicts, reviews complete, no blockers).
  - For an ML training job, this can be when the loss is unstable or the instance is preempted.
- Determine situations where the monitoring has to update what it is tracking. For example, for monitoring PRs, the latest commit hash may change as you push new commits.

### Writing

- The monitoring script should poll every 30s. `watch_pr.py` defaults to
  `--poll-interval 30`. Lower intervals cause GitHub rate limits, especially
  with more than one watcher on the same token.
- Based on the planning, exit immediately on terminal conditions with FAILED, DONE, or CANCELLED, and log ACTION_REQUIRED for wakeups.
- Send all debug diagnostics — both your watcher's own trace and the monitored job's output — to a file, so a log line can never be mistaken for DONE, FAILED, or CANCELLED.
- The script should fail as early as possible. Emit a FAILED token immediately when any required condition reaches terminal failure. For example, if you are waiting on CI and any of them fail, emit FAILED immediately.
- Write the script to a durable location such as ~/.grok and name it something clear such as `ci_watcher.sh`.
- Key every log file the script writes on the pid or session id of the thing being watched. The paths are otherwise fixed, so a second job of the same kind silently clobbers the first one's log.

## Handling wake-ups

- Address errors or actionable events immediately. Look through the logs and debug the issue thoroughly before settling on a root cause, as long-running processes are generally expensive. Resubmit the job once it is fixed:
  - For PRs, this means repushing the changes and restarting CI (if needed).
  - For jobs, requeue or relaunch the job.
  - Always restart the monitor or loop so that it points at the new PR or job.
- If there are multiple jobs running, start debugging immediately when any jobs fail. Minimize total wall-time with completing tasks.

## Restarts

- Whenever you relaunch a job, always update the monitor.
- Monitors have a maximum 10-hour time limit, so be sure to restart them if you hit the time limit and if the task being monitored is still running.
- When you spawn a new monitor, make sure to kill any previous ones that the new one replaces. For example, if you fix a training run and respawn it, be sure to kill previous monitors, as irrelevant wakeups are expensive.

## Cleanup

- If a monitor is in a terminal state, kill the monitor, the loop, and the job. Dangling processes such as unkilled broken training runs are expensive. Then, address all issues if present.
- If an outdated monitor wakes you — that is, it is attached to an old or dead run — make sure to kill it.
- Do not leave detached workers, duplicate pollers, or orphaned watcher processes behind.

### Example: maintaining a dev server

Suppose you just made some changes to the user's frontend code and would like to spin it up to test it. While you're testing it, you would like to know if the server goes down for any reason (if you made changes, for example). This is a great use case for the monitor tool. First start a React app in a background terminal, which reports its pid:

```
run_terminal_command(
  command="echo $$; npm start >~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/dev_server_$$.log 2>&1",
  timeout=0,
  description="Start the dev server on :3000",
  background=true
) # prints the pid 123456789
```

There are no terminal states, but there are two actionable events from the watcher: `http://localhost:3000` coming up and going down.

You want to be notified as soon as it is up so you can use it, and you want to be woken when it stops so you can address it — fix the code, restart the server, free the port. Both down paths quote the tail of the server's log, so the wakeup arrives with the error already in hand. Polling every 5s is a good cadence since you want to quickly fix it if it is down, and it is not expensive to poll.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Log paths are keyed on the server pid so two dev servers cannot clobber each other.
PID=$1 URL=http://localhost:3000 DIR=~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks
LOG=$DIR/dev_server_$PID.log
up() { curl -fsS -o /dev/null --max-time 5 "$URL" 2>>"$DIR/watch_dev_server_$PID.log"; }
why() { tail -20 "$LOG" | tr -d '\r' | tr '\n' ' '; }

until up; do
  kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null || { echo "FAILED: pid $PID exited before $URL came up: $(why)"; exit 1; }
  sleep 5
done
echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $URL is up"

while :; do
  sleep 5
  up || { echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $URL is down: $(why)"; until up; do sleep 5; done; }
done
```
